props.title: He Walked by Night
props.initialSlug: Ruthless killer leads LA cops on deadly manhunt

sections.content: He Walked by Night (1948) revolutionized the police procedural genre with its documentary-style realism and shadowy noir aesthetics. Shot by cinematographer John Alton, the film's innovative use of Los Angeles storm drains for its climactic chase sequence directly influenced The Third Man (1949) and laid groundwork for gritty police dramas like Dragnet (1951). Based on actual LAPD cases, it follows the manhunt for a brilliant but psychopathic burglar, featuring groundbreaking forensics techniques that would become procedural staples.

sections.content: The film's technical innovations went far beyond its story. Director Alfred Werker (with uncredited assistance from Anthony Mann) pioneered handheld camera techniques during chase sequences, creating an immediacy that influenced cinema vérité. Jack Webb, who played a forensics expert in the film, was so inspired by the procedural aspects that he created Dragnet (1951), establishing conventions still used in police dramas today.

The villain, played with chilling precision by Richard Basehart, redefined the criminal mastermind archetype. Unlike the flamboyant gangsters of earlier crime films like Little Caesar (1931), Basehart's Roy Martin is cold, methodical, and technically skilled - a prototype for modern screen psychopaths that influenced characters from The Day of the Jackal (1973) to Heat (1995). sections.content: John Alton's revolutionary cinematography in He Walked by Night established new standards for low-key lighting and location shooting. The film's dramatic use of shadows and practical light sources influenced countless noir films and modern thrillers. The storm drain sequence, shot in actual Los Angeles tunnels, created a template for underground pursuit scenes, echoing through films like The Third Man (1949) and even The Fugitive (1993).
